meta.title: Who really said "Easy Writing's Vile Hard Reading"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Hemingway. The couplet is Richard Brinsley Sheridan's, from Clio's Protest (composed 1771, printed 1772). Hemingway only quoted a later variant.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Easy Writing's Vile Hard Reading'?
meta.ogDescription: Richard Brinsley Sheridan wrote it in Clio's Protest. Hemingway said a different line, 'Easy writing makes hard reading', recorded in 1947.

answer.label: Not Ernest Hemingway — actually Richard Brinsley Sheridan
answer.authorDates: 1751–1816 · Anglo-Irish playwright, poet and Whig MP
answer.sourceLine: The line is the second half of a couplet in Sheridan’s satirical poem “Clio’s Protest; or, The Picture Varnished” — composed in 1771 and printed anonymously in 1772: “You write with ease, to shew your breeding; / But easy writing’s vile hard reading.” Quote Investigator ↗ finds Hemingway using only a reworded version and concludes he spoke the adage after it was already in circulation — the couplet predates his birth by more than a century.

source.excerpt:
You write with ease, to shew your breeding;
But easy writing’s vile hard reading.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the couplet to Sheridan’s “Clio’s Protest,” composed 1771 and distributed in 1772 in an anonymous London collection, and lists no earlier source for the wording.

Thomas Moore’s 1825 life of Sheridan quotes the couplet as “You write with ease, to show your breeding, / But easy writing’s curst hard reading” — readable in the Project Gutenberg text ↗, where Moore notes how many people quote the line without knowing its source.
Wikiquote ↗ lists both wordings under Sheridan, citing Clio’s Protest and, for the “vile” form, the Concise Oxford Dictionary of Quotations via Moore’s Life of Sheridan.
The Hemingway line is a different sentence. Wikiquote ↗ records only “Easy writing makes hard reading,” sourced to Samuel Putnam’s Paris Was Our Mistress (1947), p. 128.
source.excerptNote: Spelling as printed in 1772 — “shew” for “show.” Later reprints swap the adjective: Thomas Moore’s 1825 Memoirs has “curst,” an 1821 magazine censored it to “d—,” and an 1835 newspaper printed “very.”

source.rightsNote: The couplet appeared in print in 1772 and the poem was published under Sheridan’s name in 1819; Thomas Moore’s Memoirs, which carries the widely reproduced “curst” version, dates from 1825. All are long past copyright and in the public domain in the United States. Note that Samuel Putnam’s 1947 memoir — the source for Hemingway’s different wording — is a separate, still-protected work; only the Sheridan couplet is free to reuse.

author.name: Richard Brinsley Sheridan
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.metaLine: 1751–1816 · Anglo-Irish playwright, poet and Whig MP
author.bio: Born in Dublin in 1751, Richard Brinsley Sheridan wrote The Rivals and The School for Scandal before he was thirty, bought a controlling share of the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane, and then spent three decades in the House of Commons as one of its most feared orators. “Clio’s Protest” is early, minor, anonymous work — a young man’s hatchet job on a rival versifier — and it is the least famous thing he wrote that everybody quotes. He died in 1816; the poem did not carry his name in print until an 1819 edition, three years after his death.

misattribution.heading: Everyone it has been pinned on
misattribution.intro: This couplet has been reassigned roughly once a century. Sheridan published it anonymously, which left it up for grabs almost immediately.

items.why: Samuel Putnam’s 1947 memoir Paris Was Our Mistress records Hemingway saying “Easy writing makes hard reading” around 1926 — a different wording, and Putnam explicitly files it under “copybook triteness” among the apothegms Hemingway dropped in conversation. Quote Investigator ↗ concludes there is substantive evidence Hemingway spoke the adage only after it was already in circulation. Wikiquote ↗ carries the Hemingway line in exactly that shorter form, never as “vile hard reading.”

An 1868 newspaper columnist hesitantly credited Byron, and an 1875 magazine article stated it outright. The likely cause is the “art of easy writing” stanza of Beppo (1818) — numbered XLVIII in the 1818 first edition and LI in the later Coleridge/Prothero text: “Oh that I had the art of easy writing / What should be easy reading!” — which you can read at Wikisource ↗. Byron uses “easy writing” and “easy reading.” He never writes “hard reading” at all.

“Easy reading is damn hard writing” is a separate proverb often confused with this one and routinely credited to Hawthorne, largely because Maya Angelou attributed it to him in interviews. Quote Investigator ↗ found no substantive evidence Hawthorne used it and provisionally credits Thomas Hood, who wrote “the easiest reading is d__d hard writing” in 1837 — in quotation marks, suggesting it was already current.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Sheridan’s, from a poem he published without his name in 1772 and that only carried his name from an 1819 edition onward — documented in full at Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: A hatchet job that outlived its target
lead: “Clio’s Protest” is not a writing manual. It is a young Sheridan’s anonymous demolition of a rival’s verse, and the couplet is the punchline of a jab: the poet in question writes fluently to advertise his gentility, and the reader pays for it. The insult is that fluency was the point — ease as social display rather than craft.

Two and a half centuries later the line survives detached from its victim, its poem and its author, as a piece of workshop advice. That detachment is exactly what made it available for reattribution: a floating aphorism with no visible parentage attaches itself to whichever famous writer is nearest, and for the twentieth century that was Hemingway.
context.detailsSummary: How the wording drifted: vile, curst, cursed, very
detailsBody: The adjective was never stable. The 1772 printing has “vile.” An 1821 New Monthly Magazine item censored it to “d— hard reading.” Thomas Moore’s 1825 Memoirs of Sheridan prints “curst.” An 1835 Philadelphia paper softened it to “very.” An 1826 North American Review notice dropped the adjective entirely: “Easy writing is hard reading.” All of these are documented at Quote Investigator ↗.

Moore, writing in 1825, already treated the couplet as ownerless — “one of those stray fragments, whose parentage is doubtful” — before restoring it to Sheridan. Its authorship was being lost within fifty years of publication, which is why every later century has had its own candidate.
context.pull: Sheridan meant it as an insult about a specific bad poet. It survives as general advice to everyone.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator credits Richard Brinsley Sheridan with 'You write with ease, to shew your breeding; But easy writing's vile hard reading,' from Clio's Protest, composed 1771 and distributed 1772; it documents Lord Byron's Beppo (1818) as the source of the Byron misattribution, and cites Samuel Putnam's Paris Was Our Mistress (1970 repr., p. 128) for Hemingway saying 'Easy writing makes hard reading' circa 1926, concluding Hemingway spoke it after it was already in circulation.

Wikiquote's Richard Brinsley Sheridan page lists 'You write with ease to show your breeding, But easy writing's curst hard reading' cited to Clio's Protest (1819), and the 'vile hard reading' wording cited to the Concise Oxford Dictionary of Quotations referencing T. Moore, Life of Sheridan (1825).

Wikiquote's Ernest Hemingway page carries 'Easy writing makes hard reading' sourced to Paris Was Our Mistress (1947) by Samuel Putnam, p. 128 — and does not carry 'easy writing's vile hard reading' in any form.

Thomas Moore's 1825 Memoirs of the Life of the Rt. Hon. Richard Brinsley Sheridan, Volume 1, prints 'You write with ease, to show your breeding, / But easy writing's curst hard reading' and describes it as a stray fragment 'whose parentage is doubtful' that many quote without knowing its source.
Byron's Beppo contains 'Oh that I had the art of easy writing / What should be easy reading!' and does not contain the phrase 'hard reading'.

The Internet Archive item is Samuel Putnam's 'Paris was our mistress; memoirs of a lost & found generation', the 1970 Southern Illinois University Press edition — the same edition Quote Investigator verified with scans. The full text is lending-restricted, so the p. 128 passage was not read directly here.

Richard Brinsley Sheridan lived 30 October 1751 – 7 July 1816, was born in Dublin, was an Anglo-Irish playwright, writer and Whig politician who owned the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane, and his works list includes Clio's Protest (written 1771, published 1819).

The Google Books volume is 'Clio's Protest; Or, "The Picture" Varnished: With Other Poems' by Richard Brinsley Sheridan — the edition Quote Investigator cites as the 1819 printing that first carried his name. The page did not display the line text itself.

Quote Investigator's companion entry on the mirror maxim 'Easy reading is hard writing' provisionally credits Thomas Hood (1837, 'the easiest reading is d__d hard writing'), finds no substantive evidence Nathaniel Hawthorne used it, and notes Maya Angelou attributed it to Hawthorne.
